playbookLede: Your D2C sales guide across 5 channels, come back to this whenever you're stuck
playbookIntro: You have five channels to sell through: Offline, Online Organic, Influencer Marketing, Performance Marketing, and B2B. Every team's path to ₹7L runs through some mix of all five. This guide goes deep on each one, the how/when/where/what, an FAQ, the playbook, and exactly what to do when you're stuck. It also covers two things that cut across every channel: inventory, and how to think about revenue and expenses at each milestone.
videoNote: A note on the videos in this guide: they're general tutorials from the wider internet, not BYOB or Mesa content, useful for the fundamentals, but always adapt the specifics to your product, budget, and campus context.

inventory.intro: For a D2C brand, inventory is the single biggest way founders accidentally lose money without realising it, either by running out of stock mid-sale, or by over-ordering and tying up cash they need for marketing and operations.

terms.body: the smallest amount your supplier will produce or sell at once. Know this before you commit; it sets your minimum cash outlay.
a small buffer beyond expected sales, so a sudden spike (a stall does unexpectedly well, a Reel goes semi-viral) doesn't leave you empty-handed.
the stock level at which you should place your next order, accounting for how long your supplier takes to deliver.
inventory that isn't selling: money sitting on a shelf instead of in your bank account.

phases.label: Discover & Validate (Wk 1-2)
phases.body: Order small. Your first order should be just enough to test demand and hit your first sales, not a bulk buy. Getting stuck with 200 units of an unproven product in Week 2 is the single most common way teams lose their working capital early.

phases.label: Build & Brand (Wk 3-4)
phases.body: Once you have real sales data, reorder based on actual velocity (units sold per week), not guesses or excitement.

phases.label: Sell & Scale (Wk 5-6)
phases.body: This is where stockouts get expensive: you're spending on ads and influencers to drive traffic, and running out mid-campaign wastes that spend. Build in a safety buffer for your fastest-moving SKU.

phases.label: Optimize & Close (Wk 7-8)
phases.body: Order specifically for the Flea Market: it's a single-day, high-footfall event, and running out by noon means leaving revenue on the table you can't get back.

inventory.system: track 3 numbers weekly: opening stock, units sold, closing stock. If closing stock is trending toward zero faster than your next order will arrive, that's your reorder signal.
avoid: Ordering a “safe” large batch upfront for a better per-unit price, before demand is proven
Not accounting for supplier lead time when reordering, running out while waiting for the next batch
Treating every unit as identical: track your best-seller separately, it usually needs reordering faster
Having no plan for slow-moving stock: bundle it or discount it, don't let it just sit

revenue.intro: Revenue without a sense of your expenses is a vanity number, you could hit ₹75K in sales and still be losing money if your costs aren't in check. Here's a simple way to think about both, at every stage.

numbers.name: Revenue
numbers.body: total sales, from your daily tracker

numbers.name: COGS (Cost of Goods Sold)
numbers.body: what it cost you to make or source what you sold

numbers.name: Marketing spend
numbers.body: ads, influencer payments, flyers, everything spent to get a sale

numbers.name: Other costs
numbers.body: packaging, shipping, transaction fees, stall fees

numbers.name: Gross margin
numbers.body: revenue minus all of the above: what's actually left

lens.focus: Spend as little as possible while you validate. Your ₹30K tranche should mostly stay unspent until product and supplier are locked, don't burn it on speculative inventory or ads yet.
lens.watchFor: Overspending on “getting ready” (branding, packaging, tools) before you've sold a single unit to a stranger.

lens.focus: Your first real cost data starts here, what does it actually cost you, in money and time, to get one sale through each channel? Start learning your rough cost-per-acquisition.
lens.watchFor: Spending on ads before your store/landing page can actually convert, that's cash burned with nothing to show for it.

lens.focus: Margin discipline matters most here: you're scaling spend on what's working, so know your ROAS and margin per channel before pouring in more money.
lens.watchFor: Chasing revenue at the cost of margin, e.g. heavy discounting that grows sales but shrinks what you actually keep.

lens.focus: This is repayment math time: know, with real numbers, that you can repay your capital by 31 Oct and still have something left. Reconcile your full P&L before the Flea Market, not after.
lens.watchFor: Treating the Flea Market as “extra” sales without planning inventory and float (change, backup UPI) for a single big day.

revenue.question: If I stopped today, could I repay what I owe?
revenue.questionBody: The one question to ask every week: “If I stopped today, could I repay what I owe?” If the honest answer is no, that's the conversation to bring to your Wednesday 1:1, before it becomes a Week 8 problem.
